rationale:
Quota today is 1 long-form, 3 Shorts and 0 carousels. Under the playbook, long-forms are broad searched questions only, and breaking news goes into Shorts.

**Long-form: L2 from the queue, Mounjaro vs Zepbound.** It's a search-demand, approved-drug format, and it fits the "Tirzepatide…" title rule. It also gets ObesityWeek's Zepbound push as a timely hook. Everything in it can be checked against the two US labels (Mounjaro PI rev. 27 Aug 2026, Zepbound PI rev. 28 Aug 2026), so it's unlikely to fail fact-check. Search-demand count: First Month (11-13) and Foundayo/Pen (11-11) already make 2 of the last 7 long videos, so today didn't have to be one. It still beats the alternatives:
- **Nausea Foods re-render:** this script was logged on 11-14, so it falls under the 30-day repeat rule for new planning. It stays a ship-ready backup for a held day.
- **EloraTZP full results:** this is breaking news with thin, conflicting company and press sources, which is exactly what keeps failing fact-check. Its population is type 2 diabetes, not obesity, so it isn't the playbook's head-to-head exception. We also ran an EloraTZP Short on 11-15.

**Shorts: 2 of the 3 are a practical moment or a felt symptom.**
- **08:00:** a pen moment we haven't done before (the two clicks, from the Instructions for Use).
- **13:00:** a felt GI symptom (burping) that has never had its own Short.
- **20:00:** a spin-off of L1, busting the common "is Zepbound stronger?" myth. The holiday-table series starts on 11-18, so 20:00 holds the funnel Short today.

None of the four repeats an angle from the last 30 days. Each goes in a different pillar and none touches cost, pharmacy or approval-status framing. Breakdown: about 50% rising (L1's ObesityWeek-hooked search demand and S3), with the rest evergreen practical topics and one myth-buster.

**Closing lines:** today is content date 11-16, so the Shorts still use the old closing order (Exp F line at 08:00 and 13:00, "Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description" last). The new 11-17 ending doesn't apply yet.

pieces.topic: Mounjaro vs Zepbound: same medicine (tirzepatide), different US-approved uses, labels and device options
pieces.angle: Same structure. Chapter 2 quotes each US PI's Section 1 indications word for word, including Mounjaro's pediatric (10+ years, T2D) indication and any cardiovascular risk-reduction indication if the 27 Aug 2026 PI lists it, plus Zepbound's chronic weight management and OSA populations exactly as printed. Name the trial programme behind each (SURPASS / SURPASS-PEDS; SURMOUNT; SURMOUNT-OSA), each with its full population. State plainly: 'In the US, Mounjaro's label is for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound's label is for weight management and obstructive sleep apnea, in the populations listed.' Chapter 5 lists only the device options printed in each PI's Dosage Forms/How Supplied section (e.g. Zepbound: single-dose pen, single-dose vial, KwikPen per the current label), with each IFU cited at its own verified URL and no amounts. Chapter 3 keeps 'different trial populations, so the tables can't be compared head to head.' Keep all the other rules (no cost, dosing, switching), the don't-switch/stop/change line, one GI line ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'), 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line, and the closing line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Mounjaro vs Zepbound, What's Different?
pieces.why: Playbook L2. A broad, search-demand question with steady demand ('is mounjaro the same as zepbound'), with the ObesityWeek Zepbound push as a hook. Every claim can be checked against the two US labels, so it should pass fact-check. | fact-check: Good evergreen, high-search explainer and safe if it stays label-only. Three accuracy risks in the angle as written. (1) The Mounjaro indication is no longer just 'type 2 diabetes in adults'. FDA has since approved Mounjaro as an adjunct to diet and exercise for glycemic control in pediatric patients 10 years and older with T2D (SURPASS-PEDS; see FDA letter https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2025/215866Orig1s039ltr.pdf). Lilly has also announced a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication for adults with T2D. Paraphrasing or shortening the indication from memory would be wrong, so copy Section 1 of the 27 Aug 2026 PI word for word, including every population and age. The same goes for Zepbound Section 1 (28 Aug 2026): copy any age or population wording exactly rather than assuming 'adults' for every indication. (2) Device list: FDA approved a 4-dose single-patient-use Zepbound KwikPen in the US on 23 Feb 2026. Take the US device options for each brand only from Section 3/16 of each PI and its own IFU URLs. Don't assume Mounjaro has a US KwikPen, and don't leave out the Mounjaro single-dose vial if the PI lists one. Each IFU needs its own URL (e.g. https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-pen-us-ifu.pdf). Never cite the PI page or a PI anchor as the IFU. (3) Chapter 2 must not imply Mounjaro is used or approved for weight loss in the US. Only say what the label says. Chapter 6 (UK/AU) is fine if it's one factual line sourced to the MHRA/TGA product information, with no market talk. Packaging note: '▶ Watch next' is a publisher instruction only. It must never appear as placeholder text in the description.

pieces.topic: Didn't hear the second click on your tirzepatide single-dose pen? What the Instructions for Use say the clicks mean
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Tirzepatide pen: didn't hear the second click? Here's what the pen guide says.' By 6 s, paraphrase or quote the US single-dose pen IFU: hold for up to 10 seconds; first click = started, second loud click = complete; a softer click may come first; keep the pen on the skin until the second loud click. Then the check the IFU gives: the gray plunger being visible means the dose was delivered. If you can't see it, follow the leaflet's printed instruction and contact the number in your IFU or your healthcare provider. Don't inject again on your own. Scope card: 'US single-dose pen only. KwikPens and vials work differently. Check the leaflet in your box.' Optional stat card: 'Zepbound label (weight-management trials): injection-site reactions 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo.' Closing in 11-16 order: the scoped don't-stop/change line, 'Not personal advice', the full prescriber line, the Exp F line, then 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'
pieces.why: A visible pen moment in the slot where our pen and injection-site Shorts win (pen blood 111, injection site 254 and 202). It's a new question, and it feeds the Pen how-to long video. | fact-check: Real 'is this normal?' moment, and the IFU answers it directly. The Zepbound single-dose pen IFU (https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-pen-us-ifu.pdf) says to press and hold for up to 10 seconds. The first click means the injection started, the second click means it's complete, and a soft click may come before the second loud click. It also says not to remove the pen until the second loud click, that the gray plunger being visible confirms the dose was delivered, and that if you don't see the gray plunger you should contact Lilly at 1-800-545-5979. The 'what to do if unsure' answer is therefore the gray-plunger check plus the IFU's own contact instruction. Don't make the main instruction 'contact your pharmacist or prescriber', though adding healthcare provider as a second option is fine. Never suggest injecting again. Fixes: (a) 'US' scope must be on screen, because UK/AU viewers mostly have the Mounjaro KwikPen, which works differently, and a US KwikPen for Zepbound now exists too. (b) The 6–8% vs about 2% injection-site figure comes from the Zepbound label's weight-management trials. Name that source and population on the stat card ('Zepbound label, weight-management trials'), or drop the line. Don't present it as true for every user of this pen, because Mounjaro's label has different rates. (c) Quote the IFU only if the IFU URL itself loads. The PI is not the IFU.

pieces.topic: Burping a lot on tirzepatide: how often the label reports belching vs placebo, and gentle habits that may help
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Burping more since starting tirzepatide? It's on the label.' By 6 s: 'Zepbound label: belching (eructation) in X%, Y%, Z% on 5, 10, 15 mg vs W% on placebo' (copied exactly), with the label's pooled population on the card: adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, in trials with and without type 2 diabetes. Separate label fact: tirzepatide delays gastric emptying (no 'so'). 'Sulfur burps' is a commonly described symptom (no cause given). Untagged gentle tips: smaller meals, eat slowly, stop at comfortably full, go easier on fizzy drinks. Red flags, then the fixed don't-stop line, then the 11-16 closing with the Exp F line.
pieces.why: A felt GI moment that has never had its own Short (the 11-10 long-form covered it only as a chapter). It stays within the playbook's practical-moment rule for 13:00 and feeds the Side Effects hub. | fact-check: Common, relatable side effect that's on the label, and a safe topic with red flags included. One population error: the Zepbound adverse-reaction table pools Study 1 (which excluded type 2 diabetes) and Study 2 (which enrolled only adults with T2D), and possibly more trials, so 'adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition' on its own is incomplete. Copy the table's exact rates and the label's own description of the pooled population, and say it includes people with and without type 2 diabetes. Don't call it 'per dose' unless the table breaks it out that way. The gastric-emptying line must stay a separate label fact, never the explanation for burping. 'Sulfur burps' gets no cause and no source tag. NHS reflux/indigestion tips go only as NHS prints them, with their live reviewed date. Fizzy drinks: tag it to NHS only if the NHS page actually says it, otherwise keep it as an untagged tip. Emergency lines as written are good. Keep 'right away' and 'with or without vomiting'.

pieces.topic: Is Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro? Correcting the myth: same molecule (tirzepatide), different approved uses
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Is Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro? Both labels list the same medicine: tirzepatide.' By 6 s: both US prescribing information documents name tirzepatide as the active ingredient. The difference is what each is approved for (each PI's Section 1 indication, copied exactly with its populations) and the trials behind each. One line: 'Side-effect rates differ between the labels because the trial populations differed, so they can't be compared head to head.' One GI line ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'). 'Same ingredient doesn't mean interchangeable for you. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' Close with 'Not personal advice', the full prescriber line, then 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' No Exp F line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Is Zepbound Stronger Than Mounjaro? #shorts
pieces.target_keyword: is mounjaro the same as zepbound
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. A myth-busting question that drives viewers to the Mounjaro vs Zepbound long video and covers the 20:00 funnel slot until the holiday series starts on 11-18. | fact-check: A worthwhile myth correction: both US labels list tirzepatide as the active ingredient, and the labels differ in approved uses and trial populations. Sentence 1 as written ('Is tirzepatide as Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro?') is awkward and would make a confusing caption. The indications must be copied from each PI's current Section 1. Mounjaro now includes pediatric T2D (10+) and may include a CV risk-reduction indication, so 'type 2 diabetes in adults' alone would be inaccurate. Don't claim the two brands come in identical strengths or devices. Stick to 'same active ingredient'. Don't call the myth 'false' in a way that implies the two are interchangeable for a given patient. Pair the correction with the don't-switch line. Separate it from L1 by putting the 'stronger?' question at the centre, not the full comparison.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) weight loss in the randomized trials: how much people lost on average in SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks), how much it varied between people, why people with type 2 diabetes lost less on average (SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial), what share of the loss was lean mass, and the habits linked to getting the most from it
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide weight loss in the trials, explained honestly. SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks) gives each dose arm against placebo with its per-arm n, 'counting everyone who started', plus the shares of people reaching 5%, 15% and 20%. Chapter 3 shows the spread between people, labelled 'about'. Chapter 4 covers SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial and not head-to-head (adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks, 10 mg and 15 mg arms against their own placebo): say only that people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less and that the paper doesn't establish why. Chapter 5 covers the DXA substudy (n=160, tirzepatide doses pooled against placebo): about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat and about a quarter was lean mass, the same split seen on placebo, and lean mass isn't pure muscle. Chapter 6 covers recommended habits (protein at each meal unless your clinician limits it, muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently), never presented as proven on tirzepatide. Chapter 7 gives questions to ask your prescriber. Weight is one health measure among many.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Weight Loss: How Much in Trials?
pieces.target_keyword: how much weight can you lose on mounjaro
pieces.why:
Playbook long-form queue #3. Broad question with strong search demand (broad videos: median 621 min vs about 39 for narrow). Built only on settled primary sources (NEJM SURMOUNT-1, Lancet SURMOUNT-2, the Zepbound PI), so it can pass fact-check the first time. No overlap with the dropped Mounjaro vs Zepbound video or today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a strong evergreen topic with real search demand, and it fits the GLP-1 pillar. The evidence base is solid: SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022), SURMOUNT-2 (Lancet 2023), Zepbound PI Section 14, and the SURMOUNT-1 DXA body-composition paper (Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025, doi 10.1111/dom.16275, PMC11965027). I confirmed the DXA paper exists, and its figures match. It had 160 participants with DXA at baseline and week 72. At week 72, body weight changed by -21.3%, fat mass by -33.9% and lean mass by -10.9% on tirzepatide. On placebo the changes were -5.3%, -8.2% and -2.6%. About 75% of the weight lost was fat and about 25% was lean mass. That split was the same for tirzepatide and placebo.

Three things in the brief need changing:
1. Chapter 5 asks for 'per-arm substudy sizes'. The DXA paper reports tirzepatide doses pooled against placebo (n=160 in total). Don't invent per-dose DXA sizes. Report the pooled tirzepatide n and the placebo n exactly as the paper prints them.
2. Chapter 5 must also say the ~3:1 fat-to-lean split was the same on placebo. If it doesn't, viewers will read the split as something specific to tirzepatide. Keep 'lean mass isn't pure muscle' (it also includes water, organs and so on). Don't claim the lean-mass loss is harmless or harmful: the paper didn't measure function.
3. Chapter 4: SURMOUNT-2 doesn't establish why people with type 2 diabetes lose less. At most, say the paper notes that weight loss is generally lower in people with type 2 diabetes, and that the reasons aren't fully established. Don't name mechanisms (for example glucose-lowering drugs or less glucose lost in urine) unless the paper's text says them. SURMOUNT-2 tested only the 10 mg and 15 mg arms. Never put SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 numbers side by side on one stat card.

Other checks:
- Saying the dose arm labels (5/10/15 mg) as trial arms is acceptable under the dosing rule, as long as each one is framed as a trial arm and comes with 'your prescriber decides yours'. Don't show any titration schedule or timeline.
- Chapter 3's spread: use only the distributions the paper or its supplement shows, labelled 'about'. Don't frame them as 'non-responders' or make predictions.
- Chapter 6 habits are general recommendations from the 2025 advisory and WHO. Never present them as trial findings.
- Keep the GI line exactly as written, and keep the don't-stop and prescriber lines.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) months 2–6: what to expect after the first month, told by experience (appetite and food noise, how stomach side effects tend to change, the shape of average weight change, hair shedding, the birth-control note around dose increases, injection-site reactions) using only the US labels and SURMOUNT-1
pieces.angle:
Tirzepatide months 2–6: what the US labels and SURMOUNT-1 say about the months after the first one. The title leads with 'Tirzepatide' (e.g. 'Tirzepatide After Month 1: What Months 2–6 Can Look Like'). Brand names appear only with their own label's data, and Mounjaro figures only if labelled as type 2 diabetes trials. Thumbnail text: 'AFTER MONTH 1' or 'MONTHS 2–6: WHAT CHANGES', with one calm labelled character and no body imagery.

Chapters stay organised by experience:
(1) Appetite: label mechanism (reduced appetite and food intake). 'Food noise' is framed as a viewer term, with no promise it stays quiet.
(2) Stomach side effects: 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'. Pooled nausea rates name the Zepbound weight-management trial pool vs placebo.
(3) Weight: SURMOUNT-1 average curve shape in words, for tirzepatide vs placebo, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, over 72 weeks. Only figures stated in text, never read off the graph. Framed as averages, not predictions, pointing to the Plateau and How Long videos.
(4) Hair shedding: 5.4% vs 0.9% (women 7.1%, men 0.5%) in the Zepbound weight trials, with a hedged link to faster weight loss. See a doctor if it's patchy or lasts.
(5) ORAL hormonal contraceptives only: tirzepatide may make them less effective for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber about non-oral or backup options. Other methods are not mentioned as affected.
(6) Injection-site reactions: 6–8% vs about 2% on placebo. Rotation tip credited to the Mounjaro/Zepbound IFU at its own URL.
(7) Questions for your prescriber, plus protein (kidney caveat) and gentle strength training, marked 'recommended'.

Safety: emergency card for severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting (get help right away), followed by the scoped don't-stop/change line. Low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea. No dose numbers, no titration and no week-by-week dosing calendar. Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
pieces.why:
Playbook queue #5 and the planned sequel to First Month. It's a broad, searched what-to-expect question that can be verified fully from the US labels and NEJM, and it doesn't repeat either dropped topic or today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a good evergreen sequel with real search demand, and it fits the channel focus. The guardrails are mostly right: no dose numbers, organised by experience, an emergency card, a hypoglycaemia caveat and scoped trial populations. It needs a few accuracy and packaging fixes first.

1) BIRTH CONTROL SCOPE: the Zepbound/Mounjaro label note covers ORAL hormonal contraceptives only, not all birth control. Tirzepatide's delayed stomach emptying may reduce how well oral contraceptives work. The label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting and for 4 weeks after each dose increase. The chapter must say 'oral' every time, on screen and in narration. It must not imply that IUDs, implants, injections, patches or rings are affected. It must not present slower stomach emptying as the proven cause; keep the label's 'may'. Keep 'ask your prescriber about backup options'.

2) TITLE / BRAND SCOPE: the working title names only Mounjaro, but most of the data (pooled nausea, hair loss 5.4% vs 0.9%, injection-site rates, SURMOUNT-1) comes from the Zepbound label and obesity trials. Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes. Lead with 'Tirzepatide'. If a brand appears, use both, or tie each number to its own label. Because the title keyword names Mounjaro, the injection-site-rotation tip must cite Mounjaro's own IFU at its own URL. Never use the PI page or a PI anchor.

3) MONTHS 2–6 FRAMING: the US labels give no month-by-month data. The weight chapter may describe the shape of SURMOUNT-1's average curve for both arms (tirzepatide doses vs placebo; adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks). Do not give figures read off the graph, even labelled 'about'. Use only timepoints the paper or label states in text. Otherwise describe the shape in words ('kept going down over months, not weeks, then levelled off later in the 72-week trial'). 'Months 2–6' lines up with the dose-escalation period, so never name which dose or which week a viewer will be on.

4) THUMBNAIL: 'MONTH 3 ALREADY?' suggests a specific month-3 event the video doesn't deliver. Use text that matches the scope, e.g. 'MONTHS 2–6: WHAT CHANGES' or 'AFTER MONTH 1'. Keep one calm labelled character and no body imagery.

5) 'Food noise' is not label wording. Present it as a viewer term. Explain the appetite mechanism in label terms (reduced appetite and food intake), with no promise that it stays quiet.

6) The hair loss figures (5.4% vs 0.9%; women 7.1%, men 0.5%) come from the Zepbound weight-management trials pool. Name that pool. Phrase the link to faster weight loss with the label's hedge ('may'). The nausea-per-dose stat must name its pool: Zepbound weight-management trials, all of whom had obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition. Never compare Mounjaro type 2 diabetes rates with Zepbound rates as if they came from a head-to-head trial.

7) Emergency card: severe stomach pain that won't go away, 'with or without vomiting', 'right away', then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Protein needs a kidney-disease caveat. Strength training should be started gently and cleared with a clinician where relevant.

8) Publisher: the 'video I'd watch next' line needs a verified Side Effects video URL in the post notes. Never use the channel home page.
